title: Explore Hospital Imaging Data
text:
Measure guide

OP-10 — Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material: The reported percentage of outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast.
OP-39 — Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates: The reported percentage of screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days.

The measures describe different processes and should not be read as a single score of hospital quality. The CMS dataset provides hospital-level reported percentages; it does not explain why a particular hospital’s value differs.

text:
Hi! I’m Mariana Comartin, a student at New College of Florida with an interest in healthcare and medical imaging.
I’m interested in becoming an ultrasound technician, so I wanted to use this data science project to explore a topic connected to my future career.

title: About
text:
About This Project
U.S. Hospital Imaging Quality is an interactive data visualization website built for a college data science project.
The website examines two measures reported by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS):

OP-10 — Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material: The percentage of outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast.
OP-39 — Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates: The percentage of screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days.

The project includes interactive visualizations, comparisons between states, and an analysis of hospitals reporting both measures.
The goal is to make the data easier to explore and understand, rather than to rank hospitals or determine which provides the best care.

title: About
text:
Important Limitations
The reported percentages describe specific outpatient imaging processes, not overall hospital quality.
Differences between hospitals may reflect patient populations, clinical circumstances, or reporting practices. The dataset does not explain why individual hospitals have different percentages.
The visualizations are intended for educational exploration and should not be used to make medical decisions or choose a hospital.

title: Outpatient Medical Imaging Quality Across U.S. Hospitals
text:
Medical imaging plays an important role in diagnosing and monitoring health conditions. However, hospitals can report different results for the same imaging measures.
This project explores outpatient imaging data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), focusing on two measures:

OP-10: Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material.
OP-39: Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates.

As someone interested in becoming an ultrasound technician, I wanted to explore how medical imaging practices vary across hospitals in the United States.

title: Outpatient Medical Imaging Quality Across U.S. Hospitals
text:
What Can We Learn?
The distributions show that reported imaging percentages vary across hospitals. Most hospitals cluster within a relatively narrow range, while some report much higher percentages.
These differences are worth exploring, but they do not automatically indicate better or worse care. Clinical circumstances and patient populations can influence reported measures.
The two measures describe different processes and should not be combined into an overall hospital quality score.

title: Hospital Comparisons
text:
Hospitals across the United States report outpatient imaging measures to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Two of these measures describe different parts of medical imaging: OP-10, the percentage of outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast material, and OP-39, the percentage of breast cancer screening examinations followed by additional imaging within 45 days.
A natural question is whether hospitals reporting higher percentages for one measure also tend to report higher percentages for the other. Because these measures concern different procedures and patient populations, any relationship must be interpreted carefully.

Hospitals across the United States report outpatient imaging measures to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Two of these measures describe different parts of medical imaging: OP-10, the percentage of outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast material, and OP-39, the percentage of breast cancer screening examinations followed by additional imaging within 45 days.
A natural question is whether hospitals reporting higher percentages for one measure also tend to report higher percentages for the other. Because these measures concern different procedures and patient populations, any relationship must be interpreted carefully.

title: Hospital Comparisons
section: What Do the Hospital-Level Data Show?
text:
What Do the Hospital-Level Data Show?









The chart includes 3,169 hospitals with valid values for both measures. The median OP-10 percentage in this group is 5.3%, while the median OP-39 percentage is 6.6%. The Spearman rank correlation between the two measures is -0.01, which describes how strongly their reported percentages tend to move together across hospitals.
The points also show that hospitals can have quite different combinations of CT and breast screening percentages. This is an important limitation of using one number to describe a facility: neither measure alone provides a complete assessment of hospital quality. Differences may reflect clinical practices, patient populations, or other factors that cannot be established from this dataset.

title: Hospital Comparisons
text:
Key Takeaway
This comparison highlights why hospital imaging statistics require context. Even when two measures are reported by the same facility, they describe different clinical processes and should not automatically be interpreted as indicators of overall performance.
For more information, visit the CMS Outpatient Imaging Efficiency dataset.

title: Mammography
text:
OP-39 — Breast Cancer Screening Recall Rates reports the percentage of screening mammograms followed by diagnostic imaging within 45 days. Follow-up may include additional mammography, ultrasound, or MRI.
A recall can be a necessary part of screening, while unnecessary follow-up can add cost and anxiety. The rate alone cannot distinguish appropriate follow-up from avoidable callbacks, and it should not be treated as a stand-alone measure of a hospital’s overall quality.
The charts below use hospitals with an available OP-39 score in the July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025 reporting period.

title: Mammography
text:
OP-39 at a Glance
These statistics summarize the reported breast screening recall percentages across hospitals. A recall means that additional diagnostic imaging followed a screening mammogram within 45 days.


3,247Hospitals reporting OP-39


6.6%Median breast screening recall rate


4.7%–8.9%Middle 50% of hospital scores



Understanding Recall Rates
A screening mammogram may identify an area that requires further examination. In these cases, a patient may be called back for additional mammography, ultrasound, or other diagnostic imaging.
Recall rates matter because unnecessary callbacks can create anxiety, extra appointments, and additional costs. However, follow-up imaging can also be essential for investigating suspicious findings.
A lower recall rate is not automatically better. Interpreting these percentages requires clinical context, including the patients being screened and the reasons for additional imaging.

title: CT Imaging
text:
OP-10 — Abdomen CT Use of Contrast Material reports the percentage of a hospital’s outpatient abdominal CT examinations performed both with and without contrast. Looking at both sets of images can be clinically appropriate in some situations, so a higher percentage is not, by itself, proof of poor care.
This CMS measure concerns one specific CT practice; it is not a measure of every CT scan or of overall hospital quality. The charts below show hospitals with an available OP-10 score in the July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025 reporting period.
